question: Classify: (1) `Icon`, (2) a search field made of a label, an input and a button, (3) the site header with logo, navigation, search and cart, (4) a checkout layout with placeholder blocks.
options: (1) molecule · (2) atom · (3) template · (4) organism
(1) atom · (2) molecule · (3) organism · (4) template
(1) atom · (2) organism · (3) page · (4) molecule
(1) token · (2) atom · (3) molecule · (4) page
explanation: Atoms are indivisible elements, molecules small groups with one job, organisms complex sections, templates layouts without real content; pages are templates with real data.

question: A team proposes reorganizing the whole app into `atoms/`, `molecules/`, `organisms/`, `templates/`, `pages/`. What is the main problem?
options: It is a by-type layout: domain code (cart, checkout) gets scattered across levels, far from its hooks and API, with no domain boundaries
React cannot import from folders with those names
Atomic Design forbids folders
Organisms cannot contain state
explanation: Atomic Design classifies generic UI. Applied to the whole app it separates code by granularity instead of by domain. Keep it for `shared/ui` or the design system; organize the app by feature.

question: Your product must support dark mode and a white-label customer with different brand colors. Which setup makes this cheapest?
options: Hex colors inside each component, changed with find and replace
A `theme` prop on every component
Components that use only semantic tokens (`color-action-primary`) mapped to primitives, so each theme just remaps token values
Separate copies of the component library per customer
explanation: Semantic tokens decouple intent from value. A theme is a new mapping of tokens, usually as CSS custom properties, and components do not change.

question: Which `Button` API is best for a design system?
options: `<Button isPrimary isLarge hasLeftIcon isCartButton onAddToCart />`
A different component for every screen: `CheckoutButton`, `HeaderButton`, `CartButton`
A button that reads the cart store to decide its label
`<Button variant="primary" size="lg" {...rest}>` that forwards native props, refs and `aria-*`, with icons passed as children or a slot
explanation: Consistent, small variant props plus native passthrough keep the component flexible and accessible. Domain knowledge (the cart) belongs in features that compose the button.

question: How do a design system and feature folders relate in a well-structured React app?
options: They are alternatives: choose one
The design system lives inside one feature, and other features import it from there
The design system (atoms, molecules) is the shared UI layer or a package; features build domain organisms from it; pages compose features
Features must not use design system components
explanation: The design system is domain-free, so it sits at the bottom (`shared/ui` or an npm package). Features and pages above it compose it with domain logic.

question: When is it worth building a separately versioned design system package instead of a `shared/ui` folder?
options: When several apps or teams must share consistent UI and need versioning, documentation and ownership of the components
Always, from the first component
Only when using TypeScript
Never: design systems are a designers' concern
explanation: A package adds release, documentation and governance cost. It pays off when consistency across multiple products or teams matters; a single app is served by a disciplined `shared/ui`.
